name: Marathi
sources: Dhongde, Ramesh Vaman & Wali, Kashi (2009). Marathi. London Oriental and African Language Library 13. Amsterdam: John Benjamins.
Pandharipande, Rajeshwari V. (1997). Marathi. Descriptive Grammars. London: Routledge.
Pandharipande, Rajeshwari V. (2003). Marathi. In Cardona, George & Jain, Dhanesh (eds.), The Indo-Aryan Languages. London: Routledge.
Masica, Colin P. (1991). The Indo-Aryan Languages. Cambridge University Press.
Lisker, Leigh & Abramson, Arthur S. (1964). A cross-language study of voicing in initial stops: acoustical measurements. Word 20(3), 384-422.
Berkson, Kelly Harper (2012). Capturing breathy voice: durational measures of oral stops in Marathi. Kansas Working Papers in Linguistics 33, 27-46.
Berkson, Kelly Harper (2013). Phonation Types in Marathi: An Acoustic Investigation. PhD dissertation, University of Kansas.
Berkson, Kelly Harper (2019). Acoustic correlates of breathy sonorants in Marathi. Journal of Phonetics 73, 70-90.
Esposito, Christina M.; Khan, Sameer ud Dowla & Hurst, Alex (2005). Breathy nasals and /Nh/ clusters in Bengali, Hindi, and Marathi. UCLA Working Papers in Phonetics 104, 82-106.

Khan, Sameer ud Dowla (2016). The intonation of South Asian languages: towards a comparative analysis. Proceedings of Formal Approaches to South Asian Languages 6, 23-36 (areal intonation pattern only).
contrasts: four-way laryngeal contrast in stops and affricates: voiceless unaspirated, voiceless aspirated, voiced, breathy voiced
alveolar affricates /ts dz dzʱ/ versus palato-alveolar affricates /tʃ tʃʰ dʒ dʒʱ/, written with the same letters च ज झ (the spelling जग is both /dʒəɡ/ 'world' and /dzəɡ/ 'live!')
plain versus breathy voiced (aspirated) sonorants /m n ɳ l ɾ ʋ/ : /mʱ nʱ ɳʱ lʱ ɾʱ ʋʱ/ (/maːɾ/ 'beat' : /mʱaːɾ/ 'a caste')
no phonemic nasal vowels in the standard language
vowel length of i and u is written but hardly contrastive; six vowel qualities, plus /æ ɔ/ in English loans
allophony: /ɖ ɖʱ/ are stops word-initially and after a nasal, flaps [ɽ ɽʱ] elsewhere; there is no separate flap phoneme
/ɭ/ is a retroflex lateral flap; it does not occur word-initially
anusvara is a homorganic nasal before a stop ([ŋ] in /tsaːŋɡlaː/ 'good'); before sibilants and /ɦ/ it is a nasalised glide [w̃], before /j/ [j̃]
/ə/ is often transcribed [ʌ] or [ɤ], more back than the Hindi schwa
/ʋ/ is a labiodental approximant, [w] after consonants
high vowels are long in final open syllables and monosyllables, short elsewhere
phonotactics: the inherent vowel is dropped word-finally after a single consonant but kept after a cluster (शब्द [ʃəbd̪ə])
medial schwa deletion is less regular than in Hindi
ज्ञ is pronounced [d̪ɲ] or [d̪nj]; ऋ is [ɾu]
the alveolar affricates occur before non-front vowels in inherited words, the palato-alveolar ones before front vowels and in Sanskrit loans

stress.rule: Prominence is usually on the first syllable, with long vowels and closed syllables attracting it; descriptions are impressionistic.
stress.cues: not established instrumentally; slight duration and pitch

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none in quality; schwa deletion in weak positions
rhythm.notes: Class and final lengthening are assumptions from the areal pattern; no measurement could be verified.

length.notes: Length of /i u/ is allophonic (long in final open syllables and monosyllables). No duration figures for geminates could be verified.

voice_onset_time_ms.source: Lisker & Abramson 1964 (velar stops only, word-initial), as cited in Berkson 2012
voice_onset_time_ms.notes: Berkson 2012 measured the lag from release to regular periodic voicing (after-closure time) over all places for four speakers: plain voiceless 17 ms, voiceless aspirated 97 ms, plain voiced 12 ms, breathy voiced 22 ms; the noisy interval up to a clear second formant was 114 ms for voiceless aspirated and 131 ms for breathy voiced bilabials.

intonation.declarative: presumably the areal pattern: a rise on each content word phrase, low at its start and high at its end, and a final fall to low
intonation.yes_no_question: final high rise; the particle kā is optional
intonation.wh_question: prominence on the wh-word, final fall
intonation.continuation: high right edge on non-final phrases
intonation.notes: I know of no published intonational phonology of Marathi that I can cite with confidence; the entries follow the pattern shared by the South Asian languages studied instrumentally (Khan 2016).

phonation: breathy voiced stops and affricates /bʱ d̪ʱ ɖʱ dzʱ dʒʱ ɡʱ/
breathy voiced sonorants /mʱ nʱ ɳʱ lʱ ɾʱ ʋʱ/, single segments and not clusters with /ɦ/ (Esposito, Khan & Hurst 2005; Berkson 2019)

problems: च and झ are always palatal ([c], [ɟʰ]): चांगला, चोर, चूक, झाड, माझा come out with palatals where Marathi has the alveolar affricates /ts/ and /dzʱ/.
ज is the fricative [z] by default (जा [zaː], राजा [ɾaːzaː]) and the palatal [ɟ] before front vowels, before य and in listed words (जग); there is no affricate [dz].
Anusvara before a stop gives a nasal vowel and no nasal consonant: चांगला [cãɡlaː], आंबा [ãbaː] for [tsaːŋɡlaː], [aːmbaː]. Marathi has no phonemic nasal vowels.
Breathy sonorants are a sonorant followed by a separate voiceless [h]: म्हणून [mhəɳuːn], न्हावी [nhaːvi], कोल्हा [koːlhaː].
/ʋ/ is the fricative [v] of the base table (phoneme v imports base1/v).
Vowel length follows the spelling of i and u.
Breathy voiced stops and h come from the Hindi base table (voiced closure plus voiceless aspiration sample); intonation uses the generic tunes.
good: schwa deletion is right in most test words (करणे, मुलगा, पुस्तक)
ज्ञ as [dɳj] and ऋ as [ɾʊ] follow Marathi, not Hindi, usage

notes: An older aspirated alveolar affricate /tsʰ/ has merged with /s/. /f/ is the usual realisation of /pʰ/; /ʂ/ occurs in Sanskrit loans and merges with /ʃ/ for many speakers; [ɲ ŋ] occur only before homorganic stops. No formant table could be verified, so vowel_formants is left out.
